reviewedBy: Claude Code, scheduled morning run, session 014MKeZYLSroNs52Qq1rExKf
reviewBasis: The abstract only, read in this run on PubMed (record 43006751) and checked against Europe PMC. The full text in the Journal of Paediatrics and Child Health is behind a subscription. The abstract is enough to decide that this is not our story, so the full text was not pursued.
proposedTitle: Rejected: YouTube videos on infant choking
proposedAngle: None. It is a careful small audit of first aid videos for babies under one. Our parent has a child aged 4 to 16 and our subject is getting a child ready for a phone. Nothing in the product gives this a proof path, and a first aid finding borrowed to make a point about YouTube would be a stretch a hostile reader would see at once.

claims.claim: Of the first 200 videos returned by one YouTube search on 20 January 2026, 40 met the criteria and were scored.
Only 18.8 percent of videos warned against blind finger sweeps.
claims.basis: Abstract, results. With 40 videos, 18.8 percent is not a whole number of videos, so the denominator for this item is something other than 40 and the abstract does not say what.

claims.claim: Popularity was not associated with quality.
claims.basis: Abstract: engagement metrics were not associated with any content score. In 40 videos, finding no association is weak evidence that there is none.

claims.claim: YouTube is unsafe for parents looking for health advice.
claims.basis: The videos were rated moderate in quality and reliability, and the technique steps were almost always shown. One search, one day, one topic.

notQuotable: every figure: the story is rejected, so nothing from it is cleared
any statement about children and YouTube in general
any statement about what parents rely on: the study scored videos and asked no parent anything
evidenceConfidence: MODERATE that the abstract describes the study fairly. Not relevant to what we publish.
limitations: 40 videos from one search on one day.
A checklist built by the authors, with no account in the abstract of how raters agreed.
Infants under one year, which is outside the ages we serve.
contradictoryEvidence: From the abstract: quality was moderate and technique steps were almost always demonstrated, which cuts against any alarm story.
From the abstract: official health institutions were 22.5 percent of uploaders, so vetted material is present on the platform.
whatThisDoesNotProve: That parents are harmed by these videos.
Anything about children using YouTube themselves.
Anything about screens, phones or readiness.
mediaMisrepresentation: Coverage was not searched. Not relevant once rejected.
gdcBeliefs: Every claim needs a proof path in the product. This has none.
unresolvedQuestions: Why the discovery scoring put this in the CORE band. It matched on YouTube and parents. Worth a look at the scoring when someone is next in that file.
